measures.existing_conditions:
The building currently operates with a traditional two-pipe fan coil system that provides either heating or cooling depending on the season. Each suite is equipped with an original fan coil unit that receives hot water from the central boiler plant during the heating season and chilled water from the central chiller and cooling tower during the cooling season.

Because the system is two-pipe, the fan coils cannot supply heating and cooling simultaneously. A full building changeover is required in the spring and fall to shift between heating and cooling modes. This limitation often results in periods of thermal discomfort during shoulder seasons, as individual suites have no ability to select heating or cooling independently.

The fan coils are original to the building and have surpassed their expected service life. Aging components, reduced reliability, and declining performance contribute to inconsistent temperature control, elevated maintenance requirements, and reduced energy efficiency
measures.measure_title: Water Source Heat Pump System Conversion
measures.notes: Replace seasonal fan-coil system with water-source heat pumps on a moderate-temperature loopallowing simultaneous heating and cooling and eliminating the central chiller.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann proposes the installation of a water source heat pump for winter and summer operation. The heat pump can be installed in the existing fan coil cabinet when the fan coils are scheduled for replacement. The existing piping can remain and be reused. The existing boiler plant can remain. The chiller is no longer required and only a fluid cooler can be installed in place of the existing cooling tower. This retrofit is ideal when the fan coils and chiller are scheduled for replacement as the incremental cost of the heat pump system compared to replacing the fan coils and chiller is marginal. The water source heat pump system is far more efficient than the existing fan coil system and is capable of heating or cooling operation at any time of the year. One consideration is the electrical supply in the suites as the heat pumps have a higher electrical demand compared to the fan coils since it consists of a compressor.

As opposed to a 2-pipe fan coil system which operates at a design loop temp of 140F during heating season and 45F during cooling season, a water source heat pump system operates between 70-90F year around, meaning that the piping does not need to be insulated and there is minimal heat loss from the piping. It also means that the boiler system will always be operating in condensing temperatures with an extremely high thermal efficiency 95%+. Also, the heat input from the boiler system is greatly reduced meaning that the boiler plant can be downsized.

 In the heating season, the heat pumps extract heat from the hydronic loop and pump it into the suite. When more heat is required than is being generated within the building and most units are operating in heating mode, supplemental heating is supplied from a central boiler plant.

 In the cooling season, the heat pumps extract heat from the suites and pump it into the hydronic loop. When most of the units are in cooling mode and the heat is not needed elsewhere in the building, the heat is rejected from the loop using a fluid cooler. As opposed to a chiller, a fluid cooler comes at a much lower upfront and maintenance cost.

 During shoulder seasons, the system is capable of heat recycling, as heat from a suite calling for cooling such as a south elevation can transfer heat directly to another suite which is calling for heating such as a north elevation. In this case, no heat is rejected or input into the system.

 This measure eliminates the need for a chiller. Water source heat pump systems with fan coil units represent a sustainable and efficient HVAC solution suitable for a wide range of applications. By harnessing the thermal properties of water, these systems contribute to energy savings, environmental responsibility, and occupant comfort.

*Further engineering review is required to confirm system configuration, equipment sizing, control strategy, and integration with existing mechanical and electrical infrastructure.

measures.existing_conditions: Garage exhaust fans are currently controlled by time schedules or manual switches, with no carbon monoxide (CO) detection system. Fans may operate even when pollutant levels are low, and at times CO concentrations can exceed recommended thresholds before fans are activated.
measures.notes: Add CO sensors to control garage exhaust fans so they operate only when pollutant levels rise, maintaining air quality while reducing fan run hours and energy use.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to install a CO-based control system for the garage exhaust fans. CO sensors would be strategically located throughout the garage and connected to fan starters or the BAS. Fans would operate only when CO concentrations exceed programmable setpoints and would shut off or reduce speed when levels are low. This approach maintains air quality while reducing fan run hours, electrical energy use and noise. Further engineering is required to determine sensor locations, control sequences and integration details.

measures.existing_conditions: The parking garage air intake is not equipped with a motorized damper. Outdoor air enters the space continuously, which can result in excessive cold air infiltration during winter conditions. This may contribute to lower garage temperatures, increased heating demand where applicable, and reduced occupant comfort near entry points. No active control strategy was observed to regulate intake airflow based on outdoor temperature or operating conditions.
measures.measure_title: Install Motorized Damper for Garage Air Intake
measures.notes: Install a motorized intake damper to reduce winter cold air infiltration and improve garage temperature control while maintaining required ventilation.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to install a motorized damper at the garage outdoor air intake, integrated with a temperature sensor and control logic to modulate airflow based on outdoor conditions. The damper would reduce unnecessary cold air infiltration during winter while maintaining required ventilation rates. Integration with the existing garage fan controls or BAS (where available) would allow coordinated operation and improved seasonal performance. This measure would help stabilize garage temperatures, reduce potential heating energy demand, and improve occupant comfort near entry areas

measures.existing_conditions: The building is served by a single interval meter and there is currently no electrical sub-metering system in place to monitor power distribution or track the electricity use of individual tenants or loads.
measures.notes: Install certified electrical sub-meters on main feeds to enable consumption-based billing and end-use tracking, typically driving 5–30% electricity savings per suite.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to install an electrical sub-metering system to measure electricity use by tenant or by major end-use. Certified sub-meters would be installed on the main feeds in electrical closets and programmed to track usage for each unit or load. Sub-metering enables fair, consumption-based billing and encourages occupants to reduce waste, typically resulting in 5–30% electricity savings per suite. Measurement Canada certified meters ensure accuracy and tamper resistance, making this a practical solution for existing multi-unit buildings where full utility meter replacement is not feasible.

measures.existing_conditions: Domestic cold water is currently pressurized by a constant-speed booster pump with a downstream pressure-reducing or regulating valve to maintain setpoint pressure. The valve introduces unnecessary head loss and wastes pumping energy, and the pump operates at full speed even when demand is low.
measures.notes: Convert the constant-speed domestic booster pump to VFD control, eliminating throttling losses and matching pressure to demand for significant pump-energy savings.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to install a variable frequency drive (VFD) on the domestic water booster pump and remove or bypass the pressure regulating valve. The VFD will control pump speed to maintain the desired discharge pressure directly, allowing the pump to slow down during periods of low demand. This reduces energy use, pump wear and noise while maintaining adequate system pressure. Further engineering is required to confirm setpoints, sensor locations and control logic.

measures.existing_conditions: The existing piping arrangement fully separates the space-heating and domestic hot water (DHW) systems. Space heating uses a primary loop with a secondary circulating loop, while the DHW system is served by an independent loop with no hydraulic or control integration. This layout limits temperature control during shoulder seasons and can lead to boiler short cycling, overheating, and reduced efficiency.
measures.measure_title: Primary–Secondary Boiler and DHW Piping Reconfiguration
measures.notes: Reconfigure heating and DHW piping to a primary–secondary layout, hydraulically separating loops to improve temperature control, boiler protection and plant efficiency.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to reconfigure the heating and DHW piping into a Primary–Secondary (P-S) hydronic arrangement. In a P-S design, the boiler primary loop circulates hot water and secondary loops draw only the flow and temperature needed for each load, including space heating zones and DHW. This provides hydraulic separation, allows individualized water temperatures, improves outdoor-air reset control, and protects boilers from low-flow or low-return conditions. With this redesign, DHW storage capacity can be reduced and an instantaneous DHW system may be introduced. When combined with a condensing boiler retrofit, the number of boilers can often be reduced, lowering capital and long-term maintenance costs. Further engineering review is required to finalize the detailed design.

measures.measure_title: Window Lifecycle Planning and Sealant Renewal (Aging Double-Glazed Units)
measures.notes: Monitor aging double-pane windows and incorporate sealant renewal and long-term glazing upgrades into lifecycle and capital planning strategies.
measures.retrofit_conditions:

Full window replacement is not considered immediately necessary; however, future glazing upgrades should be evaluated in alignment with reserve fund studies and envelope lifecycle planning. Proactive lifecycle management will help maintain thermal performance, occupant comfort, and overall energy efficiency over time.

New glazing systems with improved low-E coatings, warm-edge spacers, and enhanced seal performance would significantly reduce heat loss, improve occupant comfort, and lower heating demand. Phased implementation can be considered to align with reserve fund planning and envelope lifecycle scheduling.

measures.existing_conditions: Common area lighting (e.g., corridors, stairwells, storage rooms, parking areas, and ancillary spaces) is primarily controlled through manual switches or time-based schedules, resulting in lighting operating during unoccupied periods. Limited occupancy-based control leads to unnecessary electrical energy use and increased lamp operating hours.
measures.notes: Install occupancy-based motion sensors for common area lighting to reduce unnecessary runtime, lower electrical consumption, and extend lighting equipment life.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends installing occupancy / motion sensors to control common area lighting where appropriate. The motion sensors would automatically turn lighting on when spaces are occupied and off or dim when spaces are unoccupied, reducing unnecessary runtime while maintaining occupant safety and visibility.

This measure would reduce electrical energy consumption, extend lamp and ballast/driver life, and lower ongoing maintenance requirements. Motion control is particularly effective in intermittently occupied spaces such as stairwells, corridors, storage rooms, and parking areas.

The cooling system include one (1) fluid cooler and were observed in observed to be in generally good mechanical condition; however, the fluid cooler is equipped with constant-speed or multi-speed fan motors that operate at discrete speeds regardless of the actual cooling load. Under part-load conditions, the fans still consume close to full power, resulting in unnecessary electrical usage and increased wear on mechanical components[BE5.1].
In addition, the suite circulation pumps and condenser water pumps operate at constant speed, with no VFDs installed. As a result, pump output does not modulate with system demand, leading to unnecessary electrical energy consumption and increased mechanical wear during part-load operation.
measures.measure_title: VFD Retrofit for Fluid cooler fan, Suite pumps and Condenser water pumps
measures.notes: Install VFDs on the cooling tower fan motors, suite circulation pumps, and condenser water pumps to enable demand-based modulation, reduce electrical energy consumption during part-load operation, lower noise and mechanical wear, and improve overall system efficiency and reliability.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
It is recommended to install variable frequency drives (VFDs) on the cooling tower fan motors. VFDs will allow fan speed to be modulated based on condenser water temperature, ambient conditions or BAS commands, so airflow more closely matches the required cooling load. Reducing fan speed yields large electrical savings due to the cubic relationship between power and speed, while also reducing noise and extending equipment life.

In addition, it is recommended to install variable frequency drives (VFDs) on the suite circulation pumps and condenser water pumps. The VFDs would allow pump speed to be modulated based on system demand, pressure, or temperature requirements, enabling flow rates to more closely match actual operating conditions. Reducing pump speed during part-load operation would result in meaningful electrical energy savings, reduced mechanical wear, and improved system reliability. Controls, sensors, and associated safeties would need to be updated and properly commissioned as part of this measure.

Each suite is equipped with an original fan coil unit that receives hot water from the central boiler plant during the heating season and chilled water from the central chiller and cooling tower during the cooling season.

Because the system is two-pipe, the fan coils cannot supply heating and cooling simultaneously. A full building changeover is required in the spring and fall to shift between heating and cooling modes. This limitation often results in periods of thermal discomfort during shoulder seasons, as individual suites have no ability to select heating or cooling independently.

The fan coils are original to the building and have surpassed their expected service life. Aging components, reduced reliability, and declining performance contribute to inconsistent temperature control, elevated maintenance requirements, and reduced energy efficiency
measures.measure_title: Water Source Heat Pump System Conversion
measures.notes: Replace seasonal fan-coil system with water-source heat pumps on a moderate-temperature loopallowing simultaneous heating and cooling and eliminating the central chiller.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann proposes the installation of a water source heat pump for winter and summer operation. The heat pump can be installed in the existing fan coil cabinet when the fan coils are scheduled for replacement. The existing piping can remain and be reused. The existing boiler plant can remain. The chiller is no longer required and only a fluid cooler can be installed in place of the existing cooling tower. This retrofit is ideal when the fan coils and chiller are scheduled for replacement as the incremental cost of the heat pump system compared to replacing the fan coils and chiller is marginal. The water source heat pump system is far more efficient than the existing fan coil system and is capable of heating or cooling operation at any time of the year. One consideration is the electrical supply in the suites as the heat pumps have a higher electrical demand compared to the fan coils since it consists of a compressor.

As opposed to a 2-pipe fan coil system which operates at a design loop temp of 140F during heating season and 45F during cooling season, a water source heat pump system operates between 70-90F year around, meaning that the piping does not need to be insulated and there is minimal heat loss from the piping. It also means that the boiler system will always be operating in condensing temperatures with an extremely high thermal efficiency 95%+. Also, the heat input from the boiler system is greatly reduced meaning that the boiler plant can be downsized.

 In the heating season, the heat pumps extract heat from the hydronic loop and pump it into the suite. When more heat is required than is being generated within the building and most units are operating in heating mode, supplemental heating is supplied from a central boiler plant.

 In the cooling season, the heat pumps extract heat from the suites and pump it into the hydronic loop. When most of the units are in cooling mode and the heat is not needed elsewhere in the building, the heat is rejected from the loop using a fluid cooler. As opposed to a chiller, a fluid cooler comes at a much lower upfront and maintenance cost.

 During shoulder seasons, the system is capable of heat recycling, as heat from a suite calling for cooling such as a south elevation can transfer heat directly to another suite which is calling for heating such as a north elevation. In this case, no heat is rejected or input into the system.

 This measure eliminates the need for a chiller. Water source heat pump systems with fan coil units represent a sustainable and efficient HVAC solution suitable for a wide range of applications. By harnessing the thermal properties of water, these systems contribute to energy savings, environmental responsibility, and occupant comfort.

measures.existing_conditions: No anti-scale thermostatic mixing valve was observed downstream of the domestic hot water storage tank during the site visit.As a result, delivery temperatures are controlled locally or through fixed settings, increasing the risk of temperature fluctuation, scalding, and scale buildup within downstream piping and fixtures.
measures.notes: Install an anti-scale thermostatic mixing valve to improve DHW temperature control, enhance occupant safety, and reduce scaling-related maintenance.
measures.retrofit_conditions: Install an anti-scale thermostatic mixing valve on the domestic hot water system to maintain safe and stable delivery temperatures while protecting downstream piping and fixtures from scale buildup. This measure improves temperature control, reduces scald risk, and lowers long-term maintenance requirements by minimizing mineral scaling within the DHW system.

measures.existing_conditions:
The domestic hot water (DHW) system is served by an indirect storage tank connected to the central boiler plant. The storage tank were observed to be original to the building and approaching the end of their expected service life. 
Aging indirect storage tanks typically require periodic internal relining and increased maintenance effort to maintain performance and water quality. As these components continue to age, maintenance requirements, the risk of unplanned service interruptions, and lifecycle costs are expected to increase.
measures.measure_title: Replace Aging DHW Storage Tank and Piping Retrofit
measures.notes: Replace aging indirect DHW storage tanks with glass-lined storage tanks to reduce maintenance requirements.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
As part of the boiler plant and hydronic system reconfiguration, Mann recommends upgrading the DHW system by:
•	Replacement of the existing aging indirect storage tank with new vertical glass-lined DHW storage tanks; 

The new storage tanks provide improved durability, reduced internal maintenance requirements, and more stable domestic hot water temperature control compared to aging indirect tanks.

measures.existing_conditions: At the present, the building relies on external utilities to provide electricity to power the building which might lead to high electrical energy costs.
measures.notes: Install net metered solar PV generated electricity to offset electricity consumption.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
The current state of the solar industry in Ontario is focused on “net metering” as power export to the grid is no longer an option. Rather than power export, net metered solar facilities use the generated electricity to offset electricity consumption within the facility. Since power export is not feasible, the system should be sized to only meet the baseload energy consumption of the building. This building has a high electrical consumption and ample roof space, which makes it a candidate for solar PV. 

A preliminary study is required to accurately estimate the system cost and savings for a Solar PV system

measures.existing_conditions: Garage exhaust fans are currently controlled by time schedules or manual switches, with no carbon monoxide (CO) detection system. Fans may operate even when pollutant levels are low, and at times CO concentrations can exceed recommended thresholds before fans are activated.
measures.notes: Add CO sensors to control garage exhaust fans so they operate only when pollutant levels rise, maintaining air quality while reducing fan run hours and energy use.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to install a CO-based control system for the garage exhaust fans. CO sensors would be strategically located throughout the garage and connected to fan starters or the BAS. Fans would operate only when CO concentrations exceed programmable setpoints and would shut off or reduce speed when levels are low. This approach maintains air quality while reducing fan run hours, electrical energy use and noise. Further engineering is required to determine sensor locations, control sequences and integration details.

measures.existing_conditions: The parking garage air intake is not equipped with a motorized damper. Outdoor air enters the space continuously, which can result in excessive cold air infiltration during winter conditions. This may contribute to lower garage temperatures, increased heating demand where applicable, and reduced occupant comfort near entry points. No active control strategy was observed to regulate intake airflow based on outdoor temperature or operating conditions.
measures.measure_title: Install Motorized Damper for Garage Air Intake
measures.notes: Install a motorized intake damper to reduce winter cold air infiltration and improve garage temperature control while maintaining required ventilation.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to install a motorized damper at the garage outdoor air intake, integrated with a temperature sensor and control logic to modulate airflow based on outdoor conditions. The damper would reduce unnecessary cold air infiltration during winter while maintaining required ventilation rates. Integration with the existing garage fan controls or BAS (where available) would allow coordinated operation and improved seasonal performance. This measure would help stabilize garage temperatures, reduce potential heating energy demand, and improve occupant comfort near entry areas

measures.existing_conditions: The building is served by a single interval meter and there is currently no electrical sub-metering system in place to monitor power distribution or track the electricity use of individual tenants or loads.
measures.notes: Install certified electrical sub-meters on main feeds to enable consumption-based billing and end-use tracking, typically driving 5–30% electricity savings per suite.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to install an electrical sub-metering system to measure electricity use by tenant or by major end-use. Certified sub-meters would be installed on the main feeds in electrical closets and programmed to track usage for each unit or load. Sub-metering enables fair, consumption-based billing and encourages occupants to reduce waste, typically resulting in 5–30% electricity savings per suite. Measurement Canada certified meters ensure accuracy and tamper resistance, making this a practical solution for existing multi-unit buildings where full utility meter replacement is not feasible.

measures.existing_conditions: Domestic cold water is currently pressurized by a constant-speed booster pump with a downstream pressure-reducing or regulating valve to maintain setpoint pressure. The valve introduces unnecessary head loss and wastes pumping energy, and the pump operates at full speed even when demand is low.
measures.notes: Convert the constant-speed domestic booster pump to VFD control, eliminating throttling losses and matching pressure to demand for significant pump-energy savings.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to install a variable frequency drive (VFD) on the domestic water booster pump and remove or bypass the pressure regulating valve. The VFD will control pump speed to maintain the desired discharge pressure directly, allowing the pump to slow down during periods of low demand. This reduces energy use, pump wear and noise while maintaining adequate system pressure. Further engineering is required to confirm setpoints, sensor locations and control logic.

measures.existing_conditions: The existing piping arrangement fully separates the space-heating and domestic hot water (DHW) systems. Space heating uses a primary loop with a secondary circulating loop, while the DHW system is served by an independent loop with no hydraulic or control integration. This layout limits temperature control during shoulder seasons and can lead to boiler short cycling, overheating, and reduced efficiency.
measures.measure_title: Primary–Secondary Boiler and DHW Piping Reconfiguration
measures.notes: Reconfigure heating and DHW piping to a primary–secondary layout, hydraulically separating loops to improve temperature control, boiler protection and plant efficiency.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to reconfigure the heating and DHW piping into a Primary–Secondary (P-S) hydronic arrangement. In a P-S design, the boiler primary loop circulates hot water and secondary loops draw only the flow and temperature needed for each load, including space heating zones and DHW. This provides hydraulic separation, allows individualized water temperatures, improves outdoor-air reset control, and protects boilers from low-flow or low-return conditions. With this redesign, DHW storage capacity can be reduced and an instantaneous DHW system may be introduced. When combined with a condensing boiler retrofit, the number of boilers can often be reduced, lowering capital and long-term maintenance costs. Further engineering review is required to finalize the detailed design.

measures.existing_conditions: The building is equipped with double-pane windows typical of its construction era. The windows were observed to be in generally fair condition at the time of the site visit. However, in aging buildings, the insulating glazing units (IGUs) may gradually lose performance over time due to seal deterioration and potential reduction of the insulating gas between panes. While no widespread failure was observed, long-term thermal performance may decline as glazing systems age.
measures.measure_title: Window Lifecycle Planning and Sealant Renewal (Aging Double-Glazed Units)
measures.notes: Monitor aging double-pane windows and incorporate sealant renewal and long-term glazing upgrades into lifecycle and capital planning strategies.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
As part of ongoing building envelope maintenance and long-term capital planning, it is recommended to monitor window performance and implement periodic re-caulking and weatherstripping renewal where required. Full window replacement is not considered immediately necessary; however, future glazing upgrades should be evaluated in alignment with reserve fund studies and envelope lifecycle planning. Proactive lifecycle management will help maintain thermal performance, occupant comfort, and overall energy efficiency over time.

New glazing systems with improved low-E coatings, warm-edge spacers, and enhanced seal performance would significantly reduce heat loss, improve occupant comfort, and lower heating demand. Phased implementation can be considered to align with reserve fund planning and envelope lifecycle scheduling.

measures.existing_conditions: Common area lighting (e.g., corridors, stairwells, storage rooms, parking areas, and ancillary spaces) is primarily controlled through manual switches or time-based schedules, resulting in lighting operating during unoccupied periods. Limited occupancy-based control leads to unnecessary electrical energy use and increased lamp operating hours.
measures.notes: Install occupancy-based motion sensors for common area lighting to reduce unnecessary runtime, lower electrical consumption, and extend lighting equipment life.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends installing occupancy / motion sensors to control common area lighting where appropriate. The motion sensors would automatically turn lighting on when spaces are occupied and off or dim when spaces are unoccupied, reducing unnecessary runtime while maintaining occupant safety and visibility.

This measure would reduce electrical energy consumption, extend lamp and ballast/driver life, and lower ongoing maintenance requirements. Motion control is particularly effective in intermittently occupied spaces such as stairwells, corridors, storage rooms, and parking areas.

Where applicable, motion sensors may be integrated with existing lighting control strategies or future centralized control systems to further enhance operational flexibility.

measures.existing_conditions:
The cooling system include one (1) fluid cooler and were observed in observed to be in generally good mechanical condition; however, the fluid cooler is equipped with constant-speed or multi-speed fan motors that operate at discrete speeds regardless of the actual cooling load. Under part-load conditions, the fans still consume close to full power, resulting in unnecessary electrical usage and increased wear on mechanical components[BE5.1].
In addition, the suite circulation pumps and condenser water pumps operate at constant speed, with no VFDs installed. As a result, pump output does not modulate with system demand, leading to unnecessary electrical energy consumption and increased mechanical wear during part-load operation.
measures.measure_title: VFD Retrofit for Fluid cooler fan, Suite pumps and Condenser water pumps
measures.notes: Install VFDs on the cooling tower fan motors, suite circulation pumps, and condenser water pumps to enable demand-based modulation, reduce electrical energy consumption during part-load operation, lower noise and mechanical wear, and improve overall system efficiency and reliability.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
It is recommended to install variable frequency drives (VFDs) on the cooling tower fan motors. VFDs will allow fan speed to be modulated based on condenser water temperature, ambient conditions or BAS commands, so airflow more closely matches the required cooling load. Reducing fan speed yields large electrical savings due to the cubic relationship between power and speed, while also reducing noise and extending equipment life.

In addition, it is recommended to install variable frequency drives (VFDs) on the suite circulation pumps and condenser water pumps. The VFDs would allow pump speed to be modulated based on system demand, pressure, or temperature requirements, enabling flow rates to more closely match actual operating conditions. Reducing pump speed during part-load operation would result in meaningful electrical energy savings, reduced mechanical wear, and improved system reliability. Controls, sensors, and associated safeties would need to be updated and properly commissioned as part of this measure.

ventilation_items.text: Ventilation for the building is provided by Two (2) make-up air (MUA) units, located in roof top, serving corridors and other public areas.
ventilation_items.title: Rooftop MUA

ventilation_items.text:
The units are equipped with supply fans with variable frequency drives (VFDs), integral gas-fired heating burners, and hydronic coils provide Heating and Cooling capacity. During the site visit one MUA unit was noted not running. The VFD, Hydronic coils and gas-fired heating burner, were observed to be in fair to good condition.

All units are equipped with heating and cooling coils served by glycol loops connected to the primary heating and cooling systems through plate and frame heat exchanger. 

All equipments appeared to be functioning as intended during the site walkthrough, with no visible signs of mechanical distress.
